summary: Josef Zubatý was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Alfred Ludwig at Charles University (~1876–1883, Ph.D.). He spent his career at Charles University, becoming a privatdozent in 1885 and Professor of Sanskrit and comparative Indo-European from 1894 to 1925.
Josef van Ess was a scholar in religious studies. He studied at the University of Bonn from 1953 to 1959 and held a post at the University of Tübingen from ~1968 to 1999.
Joseph Ammann was an Indology scholar who studied under Othmar Frank. In 1836, he worked as a teacher at the Hans-Carossa-Gymnasium Landshut.

Joseph Campbell worked in religious studies. He studied at Dartmouth, Columbia (B.A. 1925, M.A. ~1925–1927), and the universities of Paris and Munich. After teaching at Canterbury School (1933), he held a teaching post at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972.
Joseph D. Markowski is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Japanology. He earned a Master of Arts at McGill University, where he studied under supervisor G. Victor Sōgen Hori (attested 2004).

Joseph Dahlmann worked in Indology and religious studies, studying under Georg Bühler in Vienna and earning a Ph.D. at Berlin. A co-founder of Sophia University, he taught there in 1913 and at the University of Tokyo from 1914 to 1924.

Joseph Dalton Hooker studied at the University of Glasgow (~1832–1839, M.D.). He held posts at the British Geological Survey (1845–1847) and served as Assistant Director and Director at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (1855–1885).

Joseph David Beglar was an engineer and archaeologist who studied at Hooghly Mohsin College and Shibpur. He served in the Bengal Public Works Department and worked for the Archaeological Survey of India as Cunningham's assistant (1871) and Bengal surveyor (1885–1890).

Joseph E. Schwartzberg was an Indology and geography scholar who earned his Ph.D. under Richard Hartshorne at UW-Madison (1960). He taught at the University of Pennsylvania (1960) and served as professor at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities from 1964 to 2000.

Joseph Edward Harry studied under Maurice Bloomfield at Johns Hopkins University (A.B. ~1883–1886). He held professorships at Georgetown College (1888–1900), the University of Cincinnati (1900–1916), and Bard College (1926–1939), and lectured at the Sorbonne (1919–1922).

Joseph Edward Lyall Brandreth worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Eton College and East India Company College (~1840–1842), and served as a Member of the Imperial Legislative Council from 1867 to 1869.

Joseph Estlin Carpenter worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at UCL, Harris Manchester College, and Zurich. He was professor (1875), President (1885–1899), and Principal (1906–1915) at Harris Manchester College, and lectured at Oxford (1914–1924).
Joseph Gabet was a scholar of Tibetology, sinology, and religious studies. He completed his studies at the Petit Séminaire de Vaux-sur-Poligny and the Grand Séminaire de Saint-Claude.

Joseph Goldstein is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Anagarika Munindra, S. N. Goenka, and various Tibetan and Theravada masters. He taught at Naropa University in 1974 and co-founded the Insight Meditation Society (1974) and Barre Center for Buddhist Studies (1989).

Joseph Hackin was an archaeologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Sylvain Lévi and Louis Finot, among others. He was a curator at the Guimet Museum (1913–1941) and directed the Maison Franco-Japonaise (1930–1933) and the DAFA (1934).

Joseph Haekel completed his Ph.D. at the University of Vienna (1931–1935). He spent his academic career there as an assistant (1935), privatdozent (1941), and succeeded Wilhelm Koppers as full professor and director in 1957.

Joseph Haroutunian was a scholar of religion and philosophy. He earned degrees from the American University of Beirut, Columbia University (Ph.D. ~1928–1932), and UTS, later teaching at Wellesley (1932–1940), McCormick Theological Seminary (1940–1962), and the University of Chicago (1962–1968).

Joseph Light Wyatt worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at St Augustine's College, Canterbury, and Christ's College, Cambridge (M.A. ~1888–1893), and became a university teacher at the University of Cambridge in 1895.

Joseph Loizzo is a scholar of Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Tibetology who studied at Amherst, Harvard, and under Robert A. F. Thurman. Attested in 2007, he founded the Nalanda Institute and served as a visiting scholar at Columbia University.

Joseph M. Kitagawa was a religious studies and Japanology scholar who earned his Ph.D. under Joachim Wach at Chicago. He spent his career at the University of Chicago (~1951–1984), serving as professor and Dean of the Divinity School.
